title.en: Perimeter and area: pi, circles, sectors and Heron's formula

text.en: Measure the distance around any wheel and divide it by the distance across. You always get a little more than 3. That constant is pi, and it has fascinated mathematicians for centuries.

Pi is the constant ratio of the circumference to the diameter of any circle. It is about 22/7 or 3.14.
The circumference of a circle is C = 2 pi r, where r is the radius.
The length of an arc subtending a central angle theta is l = 2 pi r x theta / 360.
The area of a triangle is half the base times the height.
Heron's formula gives the area from the three sides a, b, c: area = square root of s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c), where s = (a + b + c)/2.
The area of a circle is A = pi r^2, and the area of a sector with central angle theta is pi r^2 x theta / 360.
Many people estimated pi: Archimedes, Zu Chongzhi with 355/113, Aryabhata with 3.1416 and Madhava with an infinite series.
Pi is irrational, so its decimal never ends or repeats; 22/7 is only a close fraction.

problem.en: Find the area of a triangle with sides 13, 14 and 15 cm.

text.en: Area = sqrt(21 x 8 x 7 x 6) = sqrt(7056).
sqrt(7056) = 84, so the area is 84 square cm.

prompt.en: What do you need for Heron's formula and why is pi special?

requiredIdeas.en: pi is the circumference to diameter ratio

commonMisconceptions.en: Using diameter in place of radius in 2 pi r

points.en: C = 2 pi r and A = pi r^2.
Arc length and sector area use the fraction theta/360.
Heron's formula finds a triangle's area from its sides.
Pi is irrational; 22/7 and 3.14 are approximations.
